title: Creating Abundance: Biological Innovation and American Agricultural Development
research_question: To what extent did biological innovation—deliberate breeding of crops and livestock and the development of pest- and pathogen-resistant varieties adapted to new soils and climatic zones—drive long-run productivity growth in American agriculture from the late 18th to the early 20th century? How does this biological channel compare in importance to mechanization, and how did westward expansion, commercialization, and public research institutions shape the pace and direction of agricultural change?
data_description: The article is a review essay discussing Olmstead and Rhode's book Creating Abundance (2008), which assembles long-run historical evidence on yields, varieties, and breeds for major US crops (wheat, corn, cotton, tobacco) and livestock (dairy cattle, beef cattle, hogs, sheep, oxen, mules, horses) from the late 18th to early 20th century, with California treated as a separate case. The review draws on US agricultural censuses (including the 1890 Eleventh Census reporting roughly 60 chickens and 179 dozen eggs per average farm), US Commissioner of Patents reports on seed and livestock experimentation, Historical Statistics of the United States (Millennial Edition), municipal ordinances (Boston 1904, New York 1912), and secondary scholarship on yields, prices, land values, dairying, and farm organization. Yield series for various crops illustrate long, nearly flat trends preceding mid-20th century 'hockey stick' breaks.
institutional_context: From the 1830s onward, American farming repeatedly confronted insect pests, fungal pathogens, soil exhaustion, and movement of cultivation into new climatic zones as settlement pushed westward across the Appalachians, Mississippi, and into California. Without continual adaptation of seeds and breeds, yields in established regions would have collapsed; instead, farmers, seed sellers, plantation owners, and public bodies introduced and selected new cultivars and livestock breeds suited to changing conditions. Commercialization of cotton, tobacco, dairy, and livestock created premiums for improved varieties, while externalities from cross-pollination, mixed seed at public gins, and the postbellum hog-round pricing system in Southern cotton blunted private incentives. Public institutions—the USDA, land-grant colleges established under the Morrill Act, agricultural experiment stations, extension services, quarantines, and government grading stations—coordinated breeding, pest control, and quality standards, complementing parallel developments at Rothamsted (1843) and Moeckern (1851).
